text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Plans for President Bill Clinton to address the Danish parliament during his short post-Helsinki summit visit to Copenhagen on March 20-21 have been shelved in favour of a presidential walkabout in the Old City. Clinton arrives in the evening of March 20, departing again for Washington in the afternoon of the following day after meeting Danish political leaders and lunching with Queen Margrethe. The far-left Unity List grouping had planned demonstrations in parliament during Clinton's visit.

--Denmark's government has given up efforts to promote developmental aid minister Poul Nielson for the post of head of UNDP - United Nations Development Programme. The European Union and UN secretary-general Koffi Annan apparently want American James Speth to stay on in the UNDP top post for another two-year term.

---Danish engineering group FLS Industries' environmental division is having trouble getting paid for a prestigious project in Poland - one of its biggest export orders ever - and is being forced to finance a 700 million crown debt on arrears in payment for the project. The Poles have apparently only paid one third of the sum so far and are paying back the rest in monthly instalments.

---The new Danish telecommunications deregulation legislation is expected to cost monopoly operator Tele Danmark such great losses in earnings that another 3,000 staff may have to go on top of the 2,500 redundancies already announced.

---According to an opinion poll, 47 percent of Danish voters want a parliamentary election this year, with 43.3 percent in favour of waiting until 1998 when general elecxtions are due in Denmark in September at the latest.
